scope: Cause/process evidence only; not validation of every attribute, TC/PC or event inclusion. Broad flood attribution does not establish a detailed hydraulic mechanism. Existing source records and unknown cause/process fields are preserved.

decisions.reason: The report documents the Cresto footbridge loss, but its match to this record remains unresolved; regional flood evidence alone cannot validate the specific bridge attribution.
Several damaged Ala di Stura crossings are documented; the provincial crossing represented by this record is not conclusively identified.
Ponte Pietra Bogone is documented as destroyed, but correspondence with this first Balme record remains unconfirmed.
Villa Sigismondi and Rio Paschiet losses are described, but the match and independence of this second Balme record remain unresolved.
Regional documentation does not conclusively identify this Chialamberto pedestrian crossing or its individual physical failure.
The specific Chialamberto provincial bridge and qualifying structural loss are not conclusively matched to the regional account.
The documented municipal bridge pier failure at Noasca has not been conclusively matched to this record; it must not be assigned to both Noasca records.
Bridge-specific retrospective reporting connects the Orzanella collapse to the flood. It reports contested proceedings, not a conclusive technical mechanism or finding of fault.
The masonry-arch collapse after prolonged adverse weather is documented, but a unique causal category or physical process is not established. The unspecified cause and trigger remain unchanged.

Ministerial report section 3.7, printed p.23, identifies the 8 May 2011 viaduct collapse and considers foundation failure the most probable cause while investigations were ongoing. This does not conclusively support the retained Material category.

ANAS tender CA 78/20, sections II.1.4 and II.2.4, explicitly identifies the Rio Enas bridge as collapsed following the 18-19 November 2013 flood. Documentation supports the broad hydraulic attribution, not a detailed mechanism.
The linked 2017 account concerns a medieval Cerami bridge at risk; it does not establish the cause of the separate recorded March 2015 collapse. Material attribution remains unconfirmed.
The March 2015 loss is distinguished from the 2009 Enna arches, but the available record does not establish a unique hydraulic failure mechanism or conclusive causal attribution.

The provincial flood-intervention register explicitly lists reconstruction of Ponte Jenga on SP109, corroborated by the provincial president's reopening account in SRC0318. Supports broad flood attribution only; no detailed process is inferred.

ARPA Piemonte report printed p.93, Fig.100, explicitly states that the Barchi bridge was completely swept away by the flood. Scour, overtopping and element-level sequence are not separately established.

Provincial emergency report prot.24231, p.1, documents a span collapse of the SP83 km0+100 Arroscia bridge during the 2-3 October flood and interruption of transit. Detailed hydraulic process remains unknown.
Bridge-specific local reporting and the surviving volunteers' account connect this Gosaldo crossing loss to the flood; no conclusive engineering diagnosis is supplied.
The contemporary report identifies San Liguori/Fosso Schettino and attributes the loss to heavy overnight rain, using conditional causal wording. No technical mechanism is established.
Contemporary reporting attributes the Terme Vigliatore crossing loss to the flood. The 2024 ANAS reopening release does not itself diagnose the 2022 failure and is not used as such proof.
The regional authority documents two collapsed Sosio arches and a planned inspection, not a settled cause. The unspecified cause and trigger are preserved.

Rai's contemporary report directly identifies the Sporzana crossing at Ozzanello and flood action. Broad hydraulic attribution is strongly supported, but not treated as a forensic determination of the detailed process.
Later bridge-specific investigation reporting identifies Ponte Ferrone and the flood-night collapse. Investigation steps are not findings of fault; the administrative-location ambiguity remains.
Contemporary reporting and the reproduced municipal closure notice identify Via Manzoni/Pisanegra during the flood. They support broad flood attribution, not a detailed primary-member diagnosis.

Contemporary reporting identifies Ponte delle Galline as swept away by the swollen stream, distinguished from the smaller Via Petrarca crossing. Detailed hydraulic sequence and exact hydrographic naming are not independently established.

Post-event reporting on Army bypass works identifies the Via Boschi/Olivetta loss in the October flood. Later removal of remnants is not confused with the original failure, whose detailed process remains unknown.
Bridge-specific contemporary reporting identifies the Elvo/Gilino crossing loss during the April flood; no conclusive technical mechanism is available.
Bridge-specific video reporting directly attributes the Neuhaus crossing loss to the swollen watercourse. It is not a technical determination of scour, overtopping or foundation failure.
